citeAs: Krizhevsky, A. (2009). Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. Technical Report, University of Toronto.
creator: Alex Krizhevsky (University of Toronto / Canadian Institute for Advanced Research)
description: CIFAR-100 is a labeled subset of the 80 million tiny images dataset, containing 600 images in each of 100 non-overlapping classes (60,000 images total). The 100 classes are organized into 20 superclasses of five classes each, and are mutually exclusive with the CIFAR-10 classes. Images are 32x32 colour images collected from the web.
name: CIFAR-100
rai:annotatorDemographics: Paid students (no further demographic details provided)
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Every label submitted by the student labelers was personally verified by the author (Alex Krizhevsky). Duplicate images were removed using L2 norm comparison.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom in-house labeling task performed by paid students
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Paid student labelers were each assigned a class and asked to examine all images found with that class name (or a WordNet hyponym) as the search term. Labelers were instructed to reject images that did not belong to their assigned class based on the following criteria: (1) the class name should be high on the list of likely answers to "What is in this picture?"; (2) the image should be photo-realistic (line drawings rejected); (3) the image should contain only one prominent instance of the object; (4) the object may be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint as long as its identity is clear. Labelers were paid a fixed sum per hour (no incentive to rush). Every label submitted was personally verified by the author. Duplicate images were removed using L2 norm comparison with a liberal rejection threshold.
rai:dataBiases: Images were originally collected via web search using English nouns from WordNet, meaning the dataset reflects the biases of web image search results (Google, Flickr, AltaVista). The search term provides only a rough label due to the unreliable nature of online image search technology. The CIFAR-100 classes are mutually exclusive with CIFAR-10 classes by design. Images tend to be symmetric about the vertical and horizontal axes due to how people take photographs.
rai:dataCollection: Images were sourced from the 80 million tiny images dataset (collected by MIT and NYU via web search). Students were paid to label a subset by filtering images found using class names and their WordNet hyponyms as search terms. Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class (or a hyponym) as the search term, rejecting images that did not belong to their assigned class. The methodology for CIFAR-100 was identical to that for CIFAR-10.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images sourced from the 80 million tiny images dataset — 32x32 colour images collected from the web by searching for every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using Google, Flickr, and AltaVista, keeping roughly the first 3000 results per search term.
rai:dataLimitations: Images are only 32x32 pixels, limiting fine-grained visual detail. The source dataset (80 million tiny images) has unreliable labels due to the nature of online image search. The CIFAR-100 dataset was only very recently completed at the time of the paper, so all classification experiments were performed on CIFAR-10 instead.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels (done during original 80 million tiny images collection). Duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs. ZCA whitening transformation was applied for model training experiments (removing 1000 least-significant principal components).
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset enables research into object recognition and deep learning on natural images. It was created to provide reliable class labels for a subset of the 80 million tiny images dataset, facilitating supervised learning experiments that were previously difficult due to unreliable web-search-based labels.
rai:dataUseCases: Object recognition and image classification benchmarking; evaluating supervised and semi-supervised learning methods on natural images; pre-training and fine-tuning deep generative models and neural networks.
